sentences.text: Euhelopus was a large, four-legged herbivore that possessed longer forelimbs than hindlimbs, a trait shared with brachiosaurids and titanosaurs. This dinosaur had a 4-meter long neck made up of 17 cervical vertebrae.

The presacral vertebrae of Euhelopus possessed a camellate pneumatic structure with many small air chambers, similar to titanosaurs. The holotype specimen includes a partial skull, lower jaws, twenty-five presacral vertebrae, and a left thighbone.

Euhelopus teeth were inclined forward, indicated by the enamel edge running toward the top and a front buttress positioned closer to the top. The axis vertebra of Euhelopus had a hollow in the back of its neural canal with three deeper pneumatic depressions.

The middle and posterior dorsal vertebrae of Euhelopus display a "K" configuration in their parapophyseal and diapophyseal laminae. Mid-presacral neural spines in Euhelopus split or bifurcated, and anterior dorsal vertebrae had a median tubercle as large as the metapophyses, resulting in a "timid" condition.
Euhelopus was originally estimated to weigh between 15 and 20 tonnes and reach an adult length of 15 meters.
In 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated Euhelopus weighed 3.5 tonnes and measured 11 meters in length.
Later studies estimated Euhelopus' mass at 5.9 tonnes by Benson et al. and 3.6 tonnes by Larramendi et al.

Euhelopus was the first dinosaur scientifically investigated from China, first seen in 1913, rediscovered in 1922, excavated in 1923, and studied by T'an that same year. The original discovery of Euhelopus remains was made by Catholic priest Father R. Mertens in 1913.
The original discovery of Euhelopus fossils was made by Catholic priest R. Mertens in 1913. Otto Zdansky excavated two skeletons of Euhelopus in March 1923.

Postaxial cervical vertebrae in Euhelopus had variably developed epipophyses and subtler preepipophyses below the prezygapophyses. In Euhelopus neck vertebrae, pleurocoels were reduced to small holes.
Presacral pneumaticity in Euhelopus extended to the ilium, which was therefore permeated by air chambers.

Most studies suggest Euhelopus is closely related to titanosaurs rather than mamenchisaurids. Euhelopus is classified within the unranked clade Somphospondyli. Euhelopus shows phylogenetic affinity to the taxon Titanosauria.
John Stanton McIntosh classified Euhelopus within the family Camarasauridae in 1990. Euhelopus is classified within the class Saurischia.

Euhelopus lived during the early Cretaceous period, approximately 129 to 113 million years ago, in what is now Asia. The Mengyin Formation dates from the Berriasian to the Valanginian stages. The Mengyin Formation was previously thought to have been deposited during the Barremian to Aptian stages, approximately 129 to 113 million years ago. Euhelopus lived from the Berriasian to the Albian stages, between 143.1 and 100.5 million years ago.
